newsitem.title: ITALY: Venice belltower stunt rings alarm on separatism.
newsitem.headline: Venice belltower stunt rings alarm on separatism.

text.p: A hint of the ridiculous surrounded Friday's surreal occupation of the belltower in St Mark's Square in Venice by eight men seeking to create an independent state in the Italian lagoon city.

The eight, who had hijacked a "vaporetto" ferry to take them and a home-made armoured vehicle down the Grand Canal to St Mark's, were arrested within a few hours when police stormed the landmark and ended the sit-in.

But while not a shot was fired, the discovery by police that the group had a sub-machine gun and a quantity of ammunition prompted politicians to caution that the incident could mark a new and potentially violent phase in Italy's internal upheavals.
Many argued that the stunt, the first of its kind, pointed to deep malaise in the affluent north at lack of federal reform of the unwieldly, centralised state.
They also said it illustrated the dangers inherent in the secessionist rhetoric of the Northern League party, even though the movement had no part in the protest.

Senate (upper house) Speaker Nicola Mancino, a southerner and former Italian interior minister, said the failure of the protest would deal a blow to all those "who believe that the questions of decentralisation...can be resolved with folklore".
But he added: "We need to take note that a state of mind exists which invites political forces to speed up reforms."

Frustration with central government bureaucracy and high taxes has been building for years in the north, including in the Veneto region around Venice where many of Italy's most thriving and dynamic small businesses are located.
The chief vehicle for discontent until now has been the Northern League, which built support by riding public outrage at corruption by established parties in the early 1990s.
Its leader, Umberto Bossi, switched last year from a federalist to a secessionist agenda, declaring a symbolic northern "Republic of Padania" at a rally in September in Venice.

His shift, accompanied by defiant talk of forming a "Padanian National Guard", has cost him votes, driven home by the loss in local elections on April 27 of control of Milan, Italy's main northern city and financial capital.
Bossi and his lieutenants were quick to condemn the Venice protest, deriding it as the work of madmen.
"Finding an armoured car and going to St Mark's Square to stand there and raise a little flag is no way to stage a revolution," Bossi told Italian radio.

The Venice protesters had no overt links with the League and issued a statement shortly before their arrest declaring themselves "soldiers" of the "Most Serene Republic" of Venice, a centuries-long power that fell 200 years ago next Monday.

Mainstream politicians, however, held Bossi at least partly to blame for whipping up a climate of strident secessionism in Italy, a country united only late in the 19th century and where national identity remains a fragile concept.

Maurizio Gasparri, a senior member of the hard-right National Alliance party, said the belltower protest had worrying parallels with early acts by extreme leftists in the 1970s that led on to Italy's worst post-war urban guerrilla violence.
"We should remember that tragedy and make sure that we immediately kill this possible terrorist virus, because that is what it is," Gasparri said.
"We should not criminalise political parties but we have to force Bossi to halt his illegal rhetoric which could find an outlet in illegal action by groups of madmen," he said.
His concerns were broadly echoed by the leader of the biggest party in Italy's centre-left government, Massimo D'Alema of the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left.
D'Alema chairs a special parliamentary commission on constitutional reform that the League has been boycotting.
The body has less than two months left to complete its work. It is meant to propose federal reforms but the issue has been pushed aside by bickering over other aspects of change.
D'Alema welcomed Bossi's condemnation of the Venice protest but said he had to follow through by taking the League back into the parliamentary reform commission.
"The country would like something more from him than a simple declaration," D'Alema said.
